criteria.note: Ball valves with red handles are visible on pipes in an open floor access hatch, beside two water meters.
Two red-and-grey lever handles are clearly visible on the pipes.
No drips, water or corrosion are visible on the valves or pipes, though the cavity is dark.

rows.note: Flat's tiled access hatch: two red-lever ball valves, filters and water meters, no visible leak or stains. Lever position must not be judged.

criteria.note: A blue ball valve is partly visible at the bottom edge, below the water meter.
A blue lever handle is visible at the bottom left of the valve.
The valve is only partly in frame and the surroundings are cluttered, so leaks or stains can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the whole valve, with its handle and pipe joints, in good light.
rows.note: Outdoor meter with a blue-lever ball valve below; the valve is partly cut off at the bottom edge, so a retake is defensible.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter (Sagemcom) close up, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible, only the meter housing and a blue button.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at a valve can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve with its handle, usually on the pipe next to the water meter.
rows.note: Electronic water meter lying on a table, not installed; no shut-off valve in frame.

criteria.note: This is an outdoor shared meter and pipe manifold on an exterior wall, not clearly the flat's own shut-off.
Small handles appear on some fittings, but they can't be tied to the flat's shut-off valve.
Pipes look weathered, but the valve isn't clearly identified and no active drip is visible.

rows.retakeHint: Go indoors and photograph the flat's main water shut-off or an appliance valve, close up, with its handle in frame.
rows.note: Black-and-white outdoor wall with several meters and small valves of a shared building; which valve is the home's is unclear and corrosion can't be judged in B/W. Corroded pipework makes fix_first defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter dial, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible, only the meter face.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at a valve cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve with its handle, usually on the pipe next to the water meter.
rows.note: Close-up of a dirty meter dial, no valve in frame (sample photo).

criteria.note: This is an outdoor excavated meter box with pipe fittings, not the flat's shut-off or an appliance valve.
No valve handle or lever is clearly visible, only pipe fittings in the pit.
No valve is in view, and the pit is too small and dim to judge leaks or stains.

rows.retakeHint: Take the photo indoors, close to the flat's main shut-off or appliance valve, with the handle clearly in frame.
rows.note: Street excavation with the utility's meter box, lid closed, no lever visible; wrong subject (the valve is inside the building).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve on a copper pipe is clearly visible.
A lever handle with a green grip is visible beside the valve.
No drips, water stains or green corrosion are visible; only normal brass tarnish and solder marks.

rows.note: Brass ball valve with a green lever on copper pipe, clean (sample photo).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve is fitted between copper pipes.
A dark lever handle with a metal bracket is visible below the valve.
Slight green corrosion marks show at the solder joint left of the valve; no active drip seen.

rows.fix: If the valve drips or is stuck, tell the property manager or maintenance company. Learn how to close it before you need to.
rows.note: Brass ball valve on copper pipe with a black lever; the lever position is ambiguous but never judged.

criteria.note: Only a close-up of a braided hose section is shown, not the run from tap to machine.
No shut-off tap is visible in the frame.
Connections are not visible; the braided section shown has no obvious damage but the whole hose can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back so the whole hose, the tap at one end and the machine connection at the other are all in frame.
rows.note: Macro of a braided steel hose only: neither the machine nor its tap is in frame.

criteria.note: A braided hose is shown near the tap end, but the machine end is cut off at the top right.
Only part of a chrome valve is visible at the bottom edge, cut off and out of focus.
The braided hose looks undamaged and dry, but the photo is blurred and the connections are partly cut off.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and take a sharp photo showing the whole hose, from the tap to the machine, with the tap fully in frame.
rows.note: Braided hose into a chrome angle valve, shallow focus; no machine in frame, so the hose is not visible from tap to machine.

criteria.note: A white P-trap under a sink is clearly visible.
A stream of water is dripping from the bottom of the trap.

rows.fix: Clean the drain or trap: lift the cover, remove hair and dirt, and rinse. Tighten a leaking nut.
rows.note: White plastic sink trap with water dripping from it: leak at the trap, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: The photo shows a loose brass valve part held up against a brick wall, not an installed dishwasher connection.
Only a loose brass fitting is shown, not an installed shut-off tap for a dishwasher.
No installed hose or connection is in frame, so leaks cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed dishwasher hose and its shut-off tap under the sink or behind the dishwasher, with both fully in frame.
rows.note: A hand holding a loose brass valve with thread tape: a loose part, not an installed connection. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: White plastic waste pipe with compression nuts and a short bottle-style trap section is visible under the sink.
No drips, standing water, stains or corrosion visible on the pipes or cabinet floor.

rows.note: Open under-sink cupboard: plastic trap with an appliance branch, dry clean floor, no leak. (No drip tray, but that is L4, not L5.)

criteria.note: Only a small white pipe stub is visible at the top; the trap is hidden behind a person in the cabinet.
The trap area is blocked from view, so leaks or blockage cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take a photo of the open under-sink cabinet with nothing in the way, showing the whole trap pipe clearly.
rows.note: A person lying in an open sink cupboard (legs only); the trap is not clearly visible. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Only the sink strainer openings are visible from above; the trap under the sink is hidden behind closed cabinet doors.
The trap can't be seen, so a blockage or leak there can't be judged. The sink basins show no standing water.

rows.retakeHint: Open the sink cabinet and photograph the pipe trap under the sink, with the whole trap and its joints in frame.
rows.note: Kitchen with the lower cupboard doors closed; the trap is not visible (sample photo).

criteria.note: This shows a braided hose under a white ceramic fixture, not a dishwasher connection.
An angle valve is visible, but it can't be confirmed as belonging to a dishwasher.
No drips or stains are visible here, but this is not the dishwasher's hose.

rows.retakeHint: Open the cupboard beside the dishwasher and photograph its hose and shut-off tap together, from a little further back.
rows.note: Toilet supply: braided hose and angle stop valve under a toilet cistern; wrong appliance for the dishwasher check.

criteria.note: A distribution board with rows of circuit breakers and blank cover panels fills the frame.
Covers appear intact with no scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts visible.
Several RCD units with TEST buttons are visible at the left and the bottom right.
Nothing is stored against or in front of the board.

rows.note: Modern ABB board: RCDs with TEST buttons, B16 breakers, labelled circuits, cover on (sample photo).

criteria.note: An old electricity meter board with fuse holders is visible in a recess.
Fuse caps are removed, leaving exposed wiring and terminals, with dark staining and old, worn components.
No RCD with a TEST button is visible on this old board.
Tools and removed fuse parts are lying in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old single-phase installation with porcelain screw-fuse holders, a removed fuse and tools on the floor: exposed parts, no RCD.

criteria.note: An empty distribution board enclosure and its separate cover are shown, with no devices installed.
The enclosure looks new and empty and the cover is off, so it's not an installed, in-use board.
No RCD or other protective devices are fitted; only the DIN rail and terminal bars are visible.
A plastic-wrapped dark item lies on the cover, but this looks like an unmounted display, not an installed board.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed fuse box in the home with its cover on and the RCD with its TEST button in view.
rows.note: An empty consumer-unit enclosure with its cover beside it, bare DIN rail, no breakers: not an installed board. fix_first (missing cover, no RCD) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A full distribution board with breakers is clearly in frame.
The front cover is off, leaving terminals, screws and wiring exposed.
Devices labelled RCBO1, RCBO2 and RC show test button symbols.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Consumer unit with its front cover removed: RCBOs and exposed terminals, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: A wall-mounted breaker panel with its door open is clearly in frame.
The cover is in place with no visible scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts.
Two breakers with yellow TEST buttons are visible at positions 6 and 12.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the panel.

rows.note: US breaker panel, door open, dead front on, handwritten circuit numbers, two GFCI breakers with TEST buttons (residual-current protection).

criteria.note: Only a single loose RCD device is shown, product-style, not a fuse box or distribution board.
Only one device is shown, so the board itself cannot be judged.
An RCD with a TEST button is clearly visible.
Isolated product image, so the area in front of a board cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take a photo of the whole fuse box or distribution board in place, with its cover open and the area in front visible.
rows.note: Product photo of an ABB RCD on a white background: not the home's board.

criteria.note: An old industrial distribution board with many enclosed switch and fuse boxes is fully in frame.
Heavy rust, peeling paint and worn, dirty enclosures are visible, though no exposed live parts are clearly seen.
No RCD with a TEST button can be seen among the old-style enclosures.
Nothing is stored in front of the board; only cables hang across its right side.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old industrial cast-metal switchgear (ASEA) with covers on but no RCD visible. A retake (not a home board) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A wall-mounted distribution board with its door open is clearly visible.
Door is open and bare terminals and busbars are exposed, with loose wiring and no inner cover visible.
Only fuses, a meter, a switch and a small breaker block are visible; no clear RCD with a TEST button.
Nothing is stored in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front. For damage, scorch marks or a missing RCD, call an authorised electrician. Don't fix it yourself.
rows.note: Open metal cabinet in an outbuilding: meter, screw fuses, main switch and exposed empty fuse bases; RCD not clearly visible.
